item.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
item.dc:creator: Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative
item.description:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

Joint statement by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

Our rationale is outlined below.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.

  1. The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.
  2. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.
  3. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.
  4. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.

Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

item.title: Our Experience at the Mathlib Reviewer Bootcamp 2026
item.dc:creator: Rida Hamadani and Hannah Scholz
item.description:
We are Hannah (she/her) and Rida (they/them), math graduate students at the University of Bonn and UPPA respectively. On 30th March 2026, we gathered with other Mathlib contributors for 4 days in Stockholm to take part in the first ever Mathlib Reviewer Bootcamp organized by Yaël Dillies and Andrew Yang with help from Michael Rothgang. The webpage with precise information on lectures and participants can be found here.

item.title: Fantastic Simprocs and How to Write Them
item.dc:creator: Yaël Dillies, Paul Lezeau
item.description:
This is the final post in our simproc series. In our first two posts, we gave an informal introduction to the concept of a simproc, and a brief overview of the inner workings of the simp tactic. The aim of this final post is to build on this by demonstrating how Lean users can write their own simprocs.

item.title: Tradeoffs of defining types as subobjects
item.dc:creator: Yaël Dillies
item.description:
It often happens in formalisation that a type of interest is a subobject of another type of interest. For example, the unit circle in the complex plane is naturally a submonoid1.

What is the best way of defining this unit circle on top of Complex? This blog post examines the pros and cons of the available designs.

Read more… (3 min remaining to read)

item.title: Simp, made simple.
item.dc:creator: Yaël Dillies, Paul Lezeau
item.description:
This is the second blog post in a series of three. In the first blog post, we introduced the notion of a simproc, which can be thought of as a form of "modular" simp lemma. In this sequel, we give a more detailed exposition of the inner workings of the simp tactic in preparation of our third post, where we will see how to write new simprocs.

item.title: The correspondence between affine group schemes and Hopf algebras
item.dc:creator: Yaël Dillies, Michał Mrugała, Andrew Yang
item.description:
This February saw the birth of the Toric project, whose aim is to build the theory of toric varieties following Toric Varieties by Cox, Little and Schenck.

We soon discovered that toric varieties contained tori, and that Mathlib didn't.

This blog post is a double announcement:

  • The unexpected prerequisite of algebraic tori was recently cleared;
  • We are looking for contributors to help with the second phase of the project, i.e. toric geometry and its relation to convex geometry.

Read more… (9 min remaining to read)
